## Area of a square

### Problem
At the left are two copies of the same isosceles right triangle $ABC$, each with an inscribed square. If the first (leftmost) inscribed square has area $S$, what is the area of the other inscribed square? Justify your answer.

![Figure for Jerry Heuer heuer-2011-p02](study/assets/asset-heuer-2011-p02-heuer-2011-p02.png)

### Solution (adapted from the official solution)
The area is $\frac{8}{9}S$.

![Figure for Jerry Heuer heuer-2011-p02-solution](study/assets/asset-heuer-2011-p02-solution-heuer-2011-p02-solution.png)

The legs of the right triangle have length $2\sqrt{S}$, so the hypotenuse is $2\sqrt{2S}$. Then the second inscribed square has side $\frac{2\sqrt{2S}}{3}$, because the smaller triangles at $A$ and $C$ are also isosceles right triangles.

Thus the area of the second inscribed square is

$$\left(\frac{2\sqrt{2S}}{3}\right)^2 = \frac{8S}{9}.$$

### Conceptual Explanation
In the first figure, the square shares the right angle at $B$. The remaining triangles along the legs are isosceles right triangles identical to each other, so the legs of $\triangle ABC$ are each $2s_1 = 2\sqrt{S}$, giving hypotenuse $2\sqrt{2S}$. In the second figure, the square has one side on the hypotenuse. The hypotenuse is partitioned into three segments: two legs of corner $45^\circ-45^\circ-90^\circ$ triangles and one square side, all equal to $s_2$. Thus $3s_2 = 2\sqrt{2S} \implies s_2 = \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}\sqrt{S}$, so $\text{Area} = s_2^2 = \frac{8}{9}S$.

### Key Technique
Partitioning the hypotenuse and legs of an isosceles right triangle using inscribed square geometry.
